title: Epoch-based allocator drift with KV prefetch windows: memory growth analysis
creator: Aria Chen
description: We observe sustained GPU memory growth on continuous-batching inference workloads when KV prefetch is enabled. Growth is not reclaimed over long tails (hours) despite apparent async free activity. This ticket tracks root-cause analysis, instrumentation additions, experiments, and a safe incremental fix path to avoid customer impact during rollout.
steps_to_reproduce: Start dedicated runtime with kv_prefetch_window=8 and continuous batching enabled (mix of short/long sequences).
Warm model KV cache by sending 1000 distinct prompts to populate cached keys, then run steady-state load at 400 req/s for 3+ hours.
Observe GPU resident memory via nvidia-smi and allocator metrics exported to grafana (allocator.resident_bytes, allocator.free_queue_len).
Capture periodic heap dumps using our allocator debug endpoint (POST /debug/allocator/dump) and nvtx traces around batch boundaries.
observations: Resident memory increases ~0.9-1.3GB/hour under mixed-batch traffic when kv_prefetch_window > 4.
Allocator free-queue length grows intermittently; async free counters show backlog on non-default CUDA streams.
Heap dumps show many small extents in 'stale' slab bins not being coalesced for long periods (epoch mismatch signature).
KV cache key residency increases faster than expected; evictions happen but memory not returned to OS / cudamempool for ~10+ minutes.
When we force a cudaDeviceSynchronize, a large portion of memory is reclaimed (suggests pending async frees completion is part of the problem).
hypothesis: Combination of (1) prefetch-induced hot-slicing of KV allocations creating many short-lived small slabs, (2) cudaMallocAsync's delayed physical free semantics on non-default streams, and (3) our epoch counter for slab reclamation not advancing on certain batching paths leads to freelist fragments not being consolidated, causing apparent leak-like growth.
proposed_fixes: Add explicit async-free draining on a dedicated 'reclaim' stream: funnel frees there and add lightweight host callbacks to kick background defragmentation when backlog exceeds threshold.
Advance allocator epoch during batch-merge operations and on the KV prefetch completion callback so slab reclamation runs even if the primary request stream is busy.
Introduce a periodic reclaim task (configurable, off by default) that performs batch coalescence and attempts cudaFreeAsync completions with a tightened timeout heuristic.
Temporarily reduce default kv_prefetch_window to 4 for Dedicated until fix is validated in canary.
Add a monitoring alarm in Grafana for allocator.resident_bytes growth > 500MB in 30m for any host.
experiments: Experiment A: Route all small-slab frees to a single reclaim stream + add host callback. Measure backlog and resident trend for 6 hours. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving/pull/7123)
Experiment B: Advance epoch in KV prefetch completion path without changing free stream. Compare coalescence rate vs baseline.
Experiment C: Disable kv_prefetch_window for a canary pod and compare memory slope; validates signal is tied to prefetch workload pattern.
Experiment D: Introduce a lightweight periodic cudaDeviceSynchronize in background (metric gated) to force pending frees; only for internal canaries to measure reclamation latency change.
test_plan: Run each experiment on a 3-pod canary (g4dn.12x or similar) for 12 hours with production-like query mixes.
Measure allocator.histogram(bin_size=64KB) over time, resident_bytes, cudaMallocAsync backlog metrics, and KV hit/eviction rates.
Run regression test suite for latency tail (p99) to ensure reclaim tasks do not add scheduling jitter that increases serving latency beyond SLO.
Post-fix: run 72-hour soak on dedicated cluster with kv_prefetch_window=8 to validate no long-term drift.
